title: Noiseless Rules
hook: The rule does not fit every case. It does not need to. It needs to produce better aggregate outcomes than discretion.
counterintuition: A noiseless rule produces worse outcomes in some individual cases by design. The expert who would have handled that case perfectly is real. But so is the expert who would have handled it badly, and both get the same discretion. The rule's advantage is not that it handles every case perfectly. It is that it removes the variance that makes the worst outcomes possible.
tryThisNow: List five recent cases of a recurring judgment and note outcome consistency. Ask: would a bright-line rule have worsened any of them? If one or fewer, the rule is probably worth testing.
keyTakeaway: A noiseless rule handles some cases worse than the ideal judge. It handles no case worse than a depleted or unlucky judge. Aggregate outcomes often favor the rule even when individual fit does not.

breakdown.fastRead:
Two sentencing charts, same offense type, two eras. The discretionary-period chart spans 18 months. The mandatory-guideline chart spans 4 months. In the right tail of the mandatory chart: a red zone marking 12 percent of cases where every reviewer agreed the sentence was disproportionately harsh. The consistency improved. The individual misfit was real.

A noiseless rule produces worse outcomes in some individual cases. The rule trades individual fit for aggregate consistency, removing the variance that makes the worst discretionary outcomes possible. The cases where the rule fits poorly are visible. The cases where discretion fails are scattered, expected, and forgotten.
breakdown.deepRead:
The argument for a noiseless rule is not that it handles every case better than a thoughtful expert would. It is that a thoughtful expert is not available for every case. The variance between what the best expert produces and what the average expert produces is the space the rule fills.

Mandatory protocols in aviation safety, sepsis treatment, and surgical checklists consistently show that removing discretion at specific high-stakes steps reduces adverse outcomes at the population level, even though any single mandated step will occasionally misfire on an unusual case. The resistance from experts is predictable: the surgeon who has never forgotten a routine step sees the checklist as an insult to their competence. They are probably right about their own performance. They are wrong about the policy. The policy applies to all surgeons, including the ones who forget things when they are tired and busy. The resistance comes from the surgeon's comparison of their own performance to the rule's performance. The relevant comparison is the rule's population performance against the population's discretionary performance.

Experts resist noiseless rules for a defensible reason and an incorrect one. The defensible reason is that the rule handles their specific cases worse than they would. The incorrect reason is that their performance is the right baseline for the policy comparison. It is not.

The rule does not need to beat the best judge to be worth adopting.

The surgical checklist does not trust the surgeon's memory. It treats every surgeon as equally likely to forget the routine step, and it is correct.
breakdown.fullRead:
Mortimer's research covers two five-year periods for the same federal offense type. Discretionary sentencing era: inter-judge variance of 18 months. Mandatory guideline era: 4 months. A red zone in the right tail of the mandatory-era chart marks 12 percent of cases where every reviewer agreed the sentence was disproportionately harsh for the specific circumstances. The consistency improved. The individual misfit was documented.

The argument for a noiseless rule is not that it handles every case better than a thoughtful expert. It is that expert performance includes more than the thoughtful ones. The rule removes the variance that makes the worst discretionary outcomes possible. Whether that trade is worth it depends on the spread and on whether exception pathways can address the mishandled cases.

"Before mandatory pre-departure checklists, crew discretion about sequence and completeness contributed to 34 percent of a studied set of taxiway incidents," Septimus said. "After mandatory checklists: 9 percent," Cordelia added. Three documented cases showed experienced captains deviating correctly during genuine emergencies. The exceptions were genuine. They were also genuinely exceptional.

At the medication safety committee's quarterly review, Aldous presented the unit comparison: two ICUs, same high-risk drug class. Mandatory-protocol ICU: dosing variance of 8 percent from optimal for matched patients. Discretionary-judgment ICU: 23 percent. In four cases, clinical discretion had produced a better outcome than the protocol would have. The protocol already had an exception pathway for all four case types.

The 12 percent of disproportionate sentences is not a rounding error. These are real outcomes for real people. The honest accounting of any noiseless rule must include them. The question is not whether the rule is perfect but whether exception pathways can address the misfit cases without restoring general discretion to the population the rule handles well.

Replace inspector discretion on 12 common violation types with bright-line enforcement rules. The pilot data: a 40 percent appeal reduction. Discretionary citations were subject to negotiation; bright-line citations were not. In 8 percent of cases, unusual building configurations made the bright-line rule less accurate than experienced inspector judgment had been. The answer was exception pathways, not general discretion restoration.

Emmeline's national tax processing report showed two numbers: 11 percent variance in final assessed tax under officer discretion for matched income profiles, 2 percent under automated bracket assignment, with appeal rates dropping 28 percent. Four percent of cases with unusual income structures were mis-categorized and required manual correction. An exception pathway, not a return to general discretion.

The safety trend chart on Fitzgerald's wall: near-miss incidents per year, declining sharply at the mandatory lockout line. From 2.4 to 0.3. Two circled points in the post-mandatory period: workers who argued the procedure was unnecessary for routine tasks they had performed safely for years. Audits found hidden energy sources in both cases. Experience had not detected them. The rule had.

Each domain produces cases where the rule fits poorly. That cost is real. But the discretionary distribution includes the tired judge and the distracted nurse alongside the thoughtful ones. The rule does not produce the best outcome for every case. It produces the worst outcome for fewer cases than discretion does.

memorableLines.text: The cases where the rule fits poorly are visible. The cases where discretion fails are scattered, expected, and forgotten.
memorableLines.why: Explains why the argument for rules is so counterintuitive: the rule's failures are salient and locatable; discretion's failures are diffuse and absorbed into normal variation.

memorableLines.text: The surgical checklist does not trust the surgeon's memory. It treats every surgeon as equally likely to forget the routine step, and it is correct.
memorableLines.why: Personalizes the rule in a way that reframes what feels like an insult to the individual as a statistically correct stance toward the population.

memorableLines.text: The rule does not produce the best outcome for every case. It produces the worst outcome for fewer cases than discretion does.
memorableLines.why: Restates the rule's advantage in terms of the floor rather than the ceiling, shifting attention from peak performance to the distribution of outcomes where it matters most.

examples.title: 18 Months to 4

planSpec.domain: mandatory minimum drug sentencing: a federal researcher analyzing aggregate sentencing outcomes before and after mandatory sentencing guidelines for the same offense type
planSpec.audience: a legal researcher studying whether mandatory sentencing guidelines reduce variance without producing unacceptable case-level injustice
planSpec.stakes: consistent justice and the individual's right to have their unique circumstances considered
planSpec.requiredBeat: discretionary sentencing variance: 18 months; mandatory guideline variance: 4 months; 12 percent of mandatory cases disproportionately harsh by reviewer consensus; chapter frames this as a genuine tradeoff, not a resolved answer

examples.scenario: Mortimer's research covers two five-year periods for the same federal offense type. In the discretionary sentencing era, inter-judge variance in sentence length was 18 months. In the mandatory guideline era, it was 4 months. A red zone in the right tail of the mandatory-era distribution marks 12 percent of cases where every reviewer agreed the sentence was disproportionately harsh for the specific circumstances involved. The consistency improved dramatically. The individual misfit was documented.
examples.whatToDo: When mandatory guidelines substantially reduce inter-judge variance, investigate whether disproportionate-sentence cases share features that a structured exception pathway within the guideline could address without restoring general discretion.
examples.whyItMatters: An 18-to-4-month variance reduction with 12 percent disproportionate cases is a genuine tradeoff. The policy question is whether exception pathways can address the 12 percent without restoring the 18-month spread.

examples.title: 34 and 9

planSpec.domain: airline crew checklist compliance: a safety culture researcher comparing accident and incident rates before and after mandatory checklist protocols in commercial aviation
planSpec.audience: an aviation safety researcher presenting to a regulatory symposium
planSpec.stakes: passenger and crew safety: discretionary safety checks produce noise at exactly the moments when consistency matters most
planSpec.requiredBeat: before mandatory pre-departure checklists: 34 percent of a set of taxiway incidents attributed to crew discretion; after: 9 percent; three documented cases of warranted deviation by experienced captains during genuine emergencies show the broken-leg exception is real and exceptional

examples.scenario: "Before mandatory pre-departure checklists, crew discretion about sequence and completeness contributed to 34 percent of a studied set of taxiway incidents," Septimus said. "After mandatory checklists, that percentage fell to 9 percent," Cordelia added. "And three documented cases showed experienced captains who deviated from the checklist correctly during genuine emergencies, whose deviations were life-saving." The three exceptions were genuine. They were also genuinely exceptional, not a reason to restore discretion across the board.
examples.whatToDo: Maintain mandatory checklist compliance while protecting the deviation authority that genuine emergencies require. Document exceptions and review them to distinguish appropriate emergency deviations from habit-based departures.
examples.whyItMatters: A reduction from 34 to 9 percent shows the rule works at the population level. Three warranted exceptions show the rule needs a deviation pathway for genuine emergencies, not a return to general crew discretion.

examples.title: 8 and 23

planSpec.domain: pharmaceutical dosing protocol: a hospital comparing patient outcomes when nurses use standard weight-based dosing protocols versus clinical judgment for a high-risk medication
planSpec.audience: a hospital medication safety officer comparing dosing error rates across two ICU units
planSpec.stakes: patient safety: dosing errors for the medication class can cause serious harm; noise in dosing is directly harmful
planSpec.requiredBeat: mandatory-protocol ICU: dosing variance of 8 percent from optimal; discretionary-judgment ICU: 23 percent; four cases where discretion produced a better outcome had exception pathways already in the protocol

examples.scenario: At the medication safety committee's quarterly review, Aldous presented the unit comparison for the same high-risk drug class. The mandatory-protocol ICU had produced dosing variance of 8 percent from optimal for matched patients. The discretionary-judgment ICU had produced variance of 23 percent. In four cases, clinical discretion had produced a better outcome than the protocol would have. The protocol already had an exception pathway for all four case types. The discretion advantage was protocol compliance expressed outside the written form.
examples.whatToDo: When mandatory dosing protocols show lower variance than discretionary judgment for matched patients, review exception cases to verify that existing exception pathways cover the cases where discretion produced better outcomes.
examples.whyItMatters: An 8 vs. 23 percent dosing variance gap shows the protocol is doing what it was designed to do. The four cases where discretion was better were already addressed by exception pathways built into the protocol.

examples.title: 40 Percent Down

planSpec.domain: building code enforcement: a municipal inspection department comparing appeal rates before and after bright-line enforcement rules replaced inspector discretion for common violations
planSpec.audience: a building department manager analyzing whether bright-line rules reduce the number of enforcement disputes
planSpec.stakes: public safety and equitable enforcement: discretionary enforcement of the same code produces different outcomes for similar properties
planSpec.requiredBeat: replacing inspector discretion on 12 common violations with bright-line rules produces a 40 percent appeal reduction; 8 percent of cases involve unusual configurations where rules were less accurate than inspector judgment; exception pathways are the fix, not general discretion restoration

examples.scenario: Would replacing inspector discretion on the 12 most common code violation types with bright-line enforcement rules raise or lower appeal rates? The pilot data showed a 40 percent reduction. Discretionary citations were subject to negotiation; bright-line citations were not. In 8 percent of cases, unusual building configurations made the bright-line rule less accurate than experienced inspector judgment had been. The 40 percent reduction was real. The 8 percent exception rate was also real.
examples.whatToDo: When a bright-line enforcement pilot produces a substantial appeal reduction, implement the rule broadly while creating a structured exception pathway for unusual case types that inspectors document during the pilot.
examples.whyItMatters: A 40 percent appeal reduction shows bright-line rules remove the negotiable ambiguity that drives disputes. The 8 percent unusual-configuration cases need an exception pathway, not general discretion restoration.

examples.title: 11 to 2

planSpec.domain: income tax bracket application: a national tax authority comparing automated bracket assignment versus officer-adjusted assessments for self-employed income
planSpec.audience: a tax authority operations director studying whether algorithmic bracket assignment reduces appeal rates and processing time
planSpec.stakes: taxpayer equity and administrative efficiency: officer discretion in bracket assignment produces inconsistent tax burdens for similar income profiles
planSpec.requiredBeat: pre-algorithmic officer discretion: 11 percent variance in final assessed tax for matched income profiles; automated assignment: 2 percent variance, 28 percent appeal rate drop; 4 percent mis-categorization requiring manual correction as the exception cost

examples.scenario: Emmeline's national tax processing report covered two periods for self-employed income bracket assignment. In the officer-discretion period, variance in final assessed tax for matched income profiles was 11 percent. In the automated-assignment period, variance fell to 2 percent and the appeal rate dropped by 28 percent. In 4 percent of cases, unusual income structures were mis-categorized by the algorithm and required manual correction. The consistency gain was large. The exception class was small.
examples.whatToDo: When an automated bracket assignment system reduces variance substantially and lowers appeal rates, create a structured manual review pathway for filers who identify income structures not handled correctly by the automated system.
examples.whyItMatters: An 11-to-2 percent variance reduction and 28 percent appeal rate drop justify automated bracket assignment. The 4 percent mis-categorization rate defines the exception class for a structured manual review pathway.

examples.title: 2.4 to 0.3

planSpec.domain: workplace safety lockout/tagout procedure: a manufacturing plant comparing injury rates with and without mandatory lockout/tagout protocol compliance
planSpec.audience: a plant safety manager who introduced mandatory lockout/tagout after a near-miss incident
planSpec.stakes: worker physical safety: worker judgment about when a machine is safe produces fatal variance; mandatory lockout removes that judgment
planSpec.requiredBeat: before mandatory lockout/tagout: 2.4 near-miss incidents per year; after: 0.3; two workers who argued the mandatory procedure was unnecessary were later found to have missed hidden energy sources in protocol audits

examples.scenario: The safety trend chart on Fitzgerald's wall shows near-miss incidents involving energized equipment declining sharply at one point: the date mandatory lockout/tagout was introduced. Before: 2.4 incidents per year. After: 0.3. Two circled points in the post-mandatory period mark the discretion-argument cases, where workers said the procedure was unnecessary for tasks they had done safely for years. Post-incident audits found hidden energy sources in both cases that the workers had not detected.
examples.whatToDo: After implementing mandatory lockout/tagout, document cases where workers argue the procedure is unnecessary and use post-incident audits to verify whether worker confidence in their discretion is matched by their ability to identify all energy sources.
examples.whyItMatters: A reduction from 2.4 to 0.3 near-miss incidents per year shows the rule addresses the failure mode that experience alone does not prevent. Two discretion-argument audits confirmed it: hidden energy sources the workers had not detected.

questions.prompt: An organization replaces a discretionary judgment process with a noiseless rule that handles 88% of cases at least as well as the median judge but produces worse outcomes in 12% of cases. What is the core logic that justifies considering this change?
choices: The rule will improve over time as the 12% exception class is identified and folded into exception pathways, eventually producing better outcomes than the discretionary process across all cases.

The relevant comparison is not the rule versus the best judge but the rule versus the distribution of all judges who exercise that discretion, including those who perform worse than the median; the rule's consistency eliminates the worst discretionary outcomes.
The 88% where the rule performs at least as well as the median judge represents the majority; majority-benefit rules are justified even when minority cases are harmed.
questions.explanation: Option A describes a future benefit that may or may not materialize; it does not address the justification at the moment of adoption. Option C confuses majority-benefit logic with aggregate-outcome logic: the 88% figure is incidental; the core justification is that the rule competes against the full distribution of discretionary performance, not against the median or the best judge. The rule eliminates the worst discretionary outcomes, which may far exceed the harm in the 12% the rule handles poorly.

questions.prompt: A hospital finds dosing variance of 8% under a mandatory protocol and 23% under clinical discretion for the same drug class. Four cases produced better outcomes under discretion than the protocol would have. What does the medication safety officer do?
choices: Maintain the mandatory protocol for the general population while investigating whether the four cases represent a pattern requiring an exception pathway, rather than treating them as grounds for restoring general discretion.
Restore clinical discretion across the ICU because the four cases show that experienced nurses identify situations the protocol cannot handle accurately.
Replace the protocol with a hybrid system where nurses choose between the protocol and clinical discretion based on their assessment of each patient's case.
questions.explanation: Four cases with better discretionary outcomes do not justify restoring general discretion if the protocol's exception pathway already covers those case types. Option B generalizes from four cases to the full population, sacrificing the 23-to-8 percent variance reduction for a problem exception pathways can address. Option C reintroduces discretion at the most consequential point, recreating the noise the protocol was designed to remove.

questions.prompt: Why are the cases where noiseless rules fail more memorable than the cases where discretionary judgment fails at the same rate?
choices: Noiseless rules fail in ways that are formally documented because rule failures trigger review processes, while discretionary failures are tracked less systematically.
Rule failures are more consequential than discretionary failures because rules apply uniformly, so a single rule failure affects many cases simultaneously.

A rule failure is attributable to the rule, making the failure visible and concentrated; a discretionary failure is distributed across individual judges and absorbed into expected variability, making it individually less salient even when it is collectively larger.
questions.explanation: Option A correctly notes documentation asymmetry but misidentifies the root cause of memorability. Option B is incorrect: a rule applies case by case, not to many cases simultaneously. The core mechanism is attribution clarity: when a rule fails, the failure is identifiable and concentrated in the rule; when discretion fails, it is distributed across many individual decisions and absorbed into the variability everyone expects.

questions.prompt: A building department replaces inspector discretion on 12 common code violations with bright-line rules, producing a 40% appeal reduction but an 8% exception rate for unusual building configurations. What is the recommended response to the 8%?
choices: Develop structured exception pathways for the documented unusual configuration types, allowing the 40% appeal reduction to stand while addressing the configuration misfit through a defined process.
Restore discretion for all 12 violation types because the 8% exception rate shows that bright-line rules systematically fail to account for building variation.
Require two-inspector review for all cases where a violation is flagged, to catch unusual configurations before an inaccurate citation is issued.
questions.explanation: Option B generalizes from 8% to restore discretion across the full population, sacrificing the 40% appeal reduction to handle a situation that a structured exception pathway can address more precisely. Option C adds inspection cost across all flagged cases to address unusual configurations that could be identified through a documentation pathway without reviewing every case twice.

questions.prompt: Before mandatory lockout/tagout, a plant averaged 2.4 near-miss incidents per year involving energized equipment. After mandatory lockout, the rate fell to 0.3. Two workers who argued mandatory lockout was unnecessary were later found in audits to have missed hidden energy sources. What does this reveal?
choices: The workers' errors show insufficient training; with better training on energy source identification, experienced workers could exercise discretion without the safety risk.
The near-miss reduction shows mandatory lockout is effective for less experienced workers; experienced workers who know their specific equipment could retain discretion without the same risk.

Experience did not provide reliable protection against the specific failure mode the mandatory rule addresses; worker confidence in their discretion was not matched by their ability to detect concealed energy sources, which the rule addresses by removing that judgment entirely.
questions.explanation: Option A attributes the failure to training rather than the limits of experience; the audit found hidden energy sources the workers missed, not procedural misunderstanding. Option B assumes experienced workers have reliable protection against the specific failure mode, which the audit evidence directly contradicts. The mandatory rule addresses precisely the failure that experience alone cannot prevent.

questions.prompt: A legal researcher documents that mandatory sentencing guidelines reduce inter-judge variance from 18 to 4 months but that 12% of cases receive sentences every reviewer agreed were disproportionately harsh. What must a policymaker evaluate?
choices: Whether the consistency gain across 88% of cases justifies the individual injustice in 12%, and whether exception pathways within the guideline structure can reduce the 12% without restoring general discretion.
Whether mandatory sentencing should be replaced with a recalibrated discretionary system that produces lower variance through training and supervision rather than rule-bound constraints.

Whether the 12% disproportionate-sentence rate should be multiplied by the total caseload to estimate the number of unjustly sentenced individuals and whether that number is an acceptable policy cost.
questions.explanation: Option B proposes restoring discretion with calibration, but calibration research suggests achieving the same variance reduction through training requires sustained feedback that discretionary systems have historically failed to maintain. Option C correctly notes that population scale matters, but the primary policy question is whether exception pathways can address the 12% within the rule structure, not whether that number is acceptable as a fixed cost.

questions.prompt: Automated tax bracket assignment reduces variance in assessed tax from 11% to 2% and drops appeal rates 28%, but mis-categorizes 4% of cases with unusual income structures. What is the correct next step?
choices: Restore officer discretion for all income bracket assignments because the 4% mis-categorization rate shows the algorithm fails to handle the full range of self-employed income structures.

Maintain the automated system while creating a structured manual review pathway for filers who identify income structures the automated system does not handle correctly, preserving the variance reduction while addressing the exception class.
Apply the automated system to straightforward cases only and route all self-employed filers to officer review, using the algorithm as a pre-filter rather than a final decision.
questions.explanation: Option A sacrifices the 98% correct-categorization rate and the 28% appeal reduction to handle 4% that can be addressed through an exception pathway. Option C reintroduces officer discretion for the full self-employed population, which was the source of the 11% variance the algorithm was designed to reduce.

questions.prompt: An experienced pilot argues that mandatory pre-departure checklists are unnecessary for pilots with more than 5,000 flight hours because their experience makes the steps automatic. How should an aviation safety researcher evaluate this claim?
choices: The claim is valid for low-risk routine tasks where automaticity is well established; mandatory checklists add value only for novel or high-risk procedures where automaticity is unreliable. Experience thresholds do not differentiate reliable automaticity from confident inattention.

The claim is valid in principle but operationally problematic because there is no reliable way to certify that a specific pilot has achieved the automaticity required to safely bypass the checklist. Flight hours are a proxy, not a measure of step-omission frequency under operational fatigue.

The claim is incorrect: experience does not reliably reduce depletion, distraction, or state-driven forgetting, which are the failure modes mandatory checklists address. Pilots who deviate correctly in genuine emergencies are a distinct population from those who skip steps out of confidence.
questions.explanation: Option A concedes the claim for routine tasks, but the research finding is that experienced pilots contribute to checklist-preventable incidents through the same mechanisms as less experienced ones. Option B acknowledges the certification problem but accepts the underlying premise. The correct response addresses the premise directly: experience does not reliably protect against depletion and distraction, which are the specific failure modes mandatory checklists prevent.

questions.prompt: A professional association argues that mandatory documentation requirements for a routine clinical procedure reduce clinician efficiency by 20% while adding marginal safety value, since experienced clinicians already follow the procedure correctly 96% of the time. Is this sufficient to overturn the mandatory requirement?
choices: No; the 4% non-compliance rate is precisely where the mandatory requirement adds value, and the efficiency cost calculation should compare the cost of the requirement against the population-level benefit of the 4% improvement, not against the satisfaction of the already-compliant 96%.
Yes; if 96% compliance is already achieved voluntarily, the mandatory requirement is adding friction for a 4% gain that does not justify the 20% efficiency cost.

Partially; the argument is sufficient to trigger a review of whether the requirement's efficiency cost can be reduced while maintaining the 4% compliance improvement, but not sufficient to eliminate the requirement without evidence that voluntary compliance can sustain at 96% without the mandate.
questions.explanation: Option B accepts the 20% efficiency cost as the relevant comparison but fails to account for the population-level benefit of the compliance improvement and the risk that voluntary compliance drifts downward without the mandate. Option C correctly identifies that the efficiency concern warrants review but does not evaluate whether the argument is sufficient to overturn the requirement. The direct analytical issue is that the requirement's value is measured against the 4% where harm is most likely, not against the 96% where it adds no marginal benefit.

reviewCards.front: How does a noiseless rule produce better aggregate outcomes even when it handles some individual cases worse?
reviewCards.back: A noiseless rule removes the variance that makes the worst discretionary outcomes possible. The best expert would handle some cases better than the rule. But the distribution of expert performance includes the depleted, biased, and unlucky alongside the thoughtful. The rule's aggregate advantage comes from eliminating the lower tail of that distribution, not from beating the upper tail.

reviewCards.front: Why do cases where noiseless rules fail attract more attention than cases where discretion fails at the same rate?
reviewCards.back: A rule failure is attributable to the rule, making it visible and concentrated. A discretionary failure is distributed across individual judges and absorbed into the variability everyone expects. The failure exists in both cases; only one of them is easy to point to.

reviewCards.front: What is an exception pathway in the context of a noiseless rule?
reviewCards.back: An exception pathway is a structured process within the rule system that addresses case types the rule handles poorly. It allows defined exceptions based on specific documented features without restoring general discretion. Exception pathways preserve the aggregate consistency gain while handling identifiable misfit cases through a structured process rather than ad hoc judgment.

reviewCards.front: What is the correct population comparison when evaluating whether to adopt a noiseless rule?
reviewCards.back: The relevant comparison is the rule's performance across the full population of cases against the distribution of all judges who would have exercised discretion, not against the best judge. Expert resistance to rules typically reflects the expert's comparison of their own performance to the rule, which is not the relevant baseline for a policy that applies to everyone with that discretion.

reviewCards.front: Why does expert experience not reliably protect against the failures that mandatory rules prevent?
reviewCards.back: Mandatory rules target failure modes driven by depletion, distraction, and state-driven forgetting, which affect experienced practitioners through the same mechanisms as less experienced ones. Experience improves performance on cases requiring judgment; it does not eliminate the occasions when the routine step is missed because the expert is tired or distracted. The rule addresses the occasion, not the judgment.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: For any recurring judgment process with significant inter-person variance, evaluate whether a bright-line rule would reduce the spread while exception pathways address the misfit cases. The question is not whether the rule handles every case as well as the best judge but whether it handles the population of cases better than the distribution of all actual judges. Measure the current spread before proposing the rule, and identify the exception class size before evaluating whether exception pathways can address it.

ifThenPlans.context: When a mandatory rule produces an outcome that the decision-maker believes is wrong for the specific case
ifThenPlans.plan: Before advocating to restore discretion, ask whether the case has a feature that could define an exception pathway trigger. If it can be defined, the fix is a structured exception, not general discretion restoration. If it cannot be defined, document it and add it to an exception pathway review rather than using the single case to overturn the rule.

ifThenPlans.context: When an expert argues that a rule is unnecessary because their personal performance exceeds the rule's performance
ifThenPlans.plan: Ask them to compare the rule's population performance against the full distribution of all practitioners who exercise that discretion, not against their own performance. The rule does not exist for the expert specifically; it exists for the distribution that includes everyone who has that discretion, including the ones who are depleted, biased, or wrong more often.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: List five recent cases of a recurring judgment you exercise and note whether outcomes were consistent. Ask: if a bright-line rule had replaced that judgment, in how many of those cases would the outcome have been worse? If the answer is one or fewer, the rule is probably worth testing as a pilot.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: For each week, identify one recurring judgment in your domain where significant inter-person variance exists. Measure the spread across the people making that judgment. If the spread is larger than case differences can explain, design the simplest possible bright-line rule that would reduce that spread and estimate how many cases would be handled worse by the rule than by the best current judge. If that number is small, an exception pathway can likely address it.
